articles.title: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
articles.description: Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat election victory would mean slower AI development.
articles.summary: Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have started to climb following an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
key_points: The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index opened higher following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.

articles.description: Fears of more AI regulation appear to have sparked fear among investors, but concerns about the industry have been growing for some time.
articles.summary: Is the artificial intelligence (AI) gold rush coming to an end, or is this simply a reality check?
key_points: That's the question which is hanging over investors, and which has prompted steep falls on the world's stock markets.
The sell-off in the US on Thursday was most dramatic on the Nasdaq, home to tech industry titans such as Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta and Apple.
It followed sweeping gains by the Democrats in this week's midterm elections in the US, which have given the party full control of Congress.

articles.description: A post-Brexit deal on food standards has raised questions over the future naming of the classic British snack.

key_points: The government is negotiating a deal on food standards in a bid to cut costs for British companies trading with Europe.
Labour ministers have been keen to talk up the potential economic benefits of the agreement, which could be announced at a summit later this month.
But the deal's requirement for Britain to adopt EU food rules in a wide range of areas has threatened to reignite sovereignty debates from the Brexit era.

articles.description: The government argues the change will help jobseekers and could help to prevent pay discrimination.

key_points: The government is planning to make pay details compulsory in adverts, with legislation on the issue being brought forward "as soon as possible".

However, one industry group said setting pay was a complex process and regulating adverts was not always suitable.
